# Dhammahadayavibhaṅga (Vb 18)

**ID:** Vb 18  
**Section:** Vibhaṅga (vb)  
**Collection:** Abhidhamma  
**Title (Pali):** Dhammahadayavibhaṅga  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/abh02m.mul17.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/abh02m.mul17.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga* ("Analysis of the Heart of the Dhamma") is the eighteenth and concluding chapter of the *Vibhaṅga*, the second book of the Theravāda Abhidhamma Piṭaka (PTS Vibh 401–436) [von Hinüber 1996]. The figurative term *hadaya* ("heart") in its title denotes the "essence," "gist," or "summary" of the teachings, parallel to the usage in later Buddhist Sanskrit texts such as the *Prajñāpāramitāhṛdaya* [Nyanatiloka 1938/1957/2007]. Hajime Nakamura notes that this final chapter is considered a later addition to the work [Nakamura 1980]. The text possesses an independent *mātikā* (matrix) and proceeds primarily as a catechism of questions and answers structuring twelve core doctrinal categories, including aggregates (*khandha*), nutriments (*āhāra*), and root causes (*hetu*) [von Hinüber 1996; Nyanatiloka 1938/1957/2007]. It also provides detailed enumerations concerning cosmology and the realms of existence, notably the life-spans of diverse classes of devas, for which reason it was later drawn upon in post-canonical thematic anthologies treating heavenly rebirth (*sagga*) [Norman 1983]. According to the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, a sectarian group known as the Vitaṇḍavādins rejected the canonical status of the *Kathāvatthu* and replaced it in their Abhidhamma basket with a work called the *Mahādhammahadaya*, which traditional commentators and modern scholars identify as being closely related or essentially identical in substance to this chapter [Nyanatiloka 1938/1957/2007; von Hinüber 1996]. Commentaries on the *Gulissānisutta* indicate that forest-dwelling monks were expected to master this text alongside the fundamental Abhidhamma mātikās [Patt 1993]. Its primary commentary forms part of the *Pañcappakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā* [von Hinüber 1996].
